446: ## Checkpoint and resume (record + re-drive policy)
447: 
448: Status (since **0.8.0**): `src/checkpoint/` (schema, atomic writer,
449: engine wiring) and `src/resume/` (validator, restore policy) ship since **0.8.0** and are
450: exercised by `test/checkpoint-schema.spec.ts`, `test/checkpoint-wiring.spec.ts` and
451: `test/resume-validator.spec.ts`. The wiring *is* called: `src/run.ts` creates one recorder per
452: run, adopts it with the engine's run object and finalises it on the terminal path,
453: while `disposeActiveState` writes one `cancelled`
454: checkpoint per live run before it aborts. No user-visible surface changed — a run gains a JSON file on disk and, on
455: failure, a warning line. This section is the contract the code implements.
456: 
457: Boundary (D-013, measured on DSH **0.2.1-rc.2**; the install, activation and settings
458: projection of this bundle were re-verified on **0.2.2-rc.3** in RSI round 8, which did *not*
459: re-measure this journaling boundary): `resume` never means engine-level resume — the shipped
460: engine journals nothing and states it as a limitation. `resumeDecision` answers a host
461: question ("should a new run re-drive the unfinished tasks from this file?") and has had no
462: production caller since **0.8.0** (as of **0.11.9** `src/resume/` is imported only by tests).
463: Recording never terminates a run: recording is best-effort and unload-bounded, and a refused
464: disk costs a warning line, never the report. There is no Command Watchdog and no Host Evidence
465: Collector as of **0.11.9** (NOT_DONE, no implementation in the tree) — those names must not
466: appear as shipped features in release notes.
467: 
468: ### Location / 位置
469: 
470: - The writer never chooses a directory: `writeCheckpoint(filePath, input)` takes the final
471:   path from the caller and creates the parent directories (`src/checkpoint/writer.ts:71`).
472: - Filename policy is `checkpointFileName(runId)`: `checkpoint-<runId>.json`, every character
473:   outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` replaced by `_`, truncated to `CHECKPOINT_LIMITS.idChars` (120),
474:   and the degenerate `''` / `.` / `..` cases folded to `checkpoint-run.json`
475:   (`src/checkpoint/writer.ts:59`). Filename derivation is total: any run id yields exactly
476:   one safe name.
477: - Default directory (wiring): `checkpointDir()` resolves an explicit `options.dir`, then
478:   `GROK_WORKFLOW_CHECKPOINT_DIR`, then `$DSH_HOME` (else `~/.dsh`) +
479:   `checkpoints/grok-workflow` (`src/checkpoint/wiring.ts:125`), and `checkpointFile(runId)`
480:   joins that with `checkpointFileName(runId)` (`:135`). The three-step shape is deliberately
481:   the one the incremental memory archive already uses (`src/memory/archive.ts:141`). There is
482:   **no setting** for it: the path is host state, not a display preference, so no configuration
483:   key selects a policy — an integration that wants a different directory passes `dir` (or the
484:   environment variable) at the call site.

486: ### Version policy / 版本策略
487: 
488: Two independent versions, each refused rather than migrated:
489: 
490: - run document: `CHECKPOINT_VERSION = 'grok-workflow.checkpoint/v1'`
491:   (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:46`);
492: - restore document: `RESUME_CHECKPOINT_VERSION = 1` with envelope kind
493:   `grok-workflow.resume-checkpoint` (`src/resume/validator.ts:28`).
494: 
495: The validator accepts exactly the version it was built with; anything else is
496: `version-mismatch` and restore is denied (`src/resume/validator.ts:208`). There is no
497: migration path and no "best effort" read: a checkpoint written by a newer build is refused
498: by an older one, by design. Bumping either number is a new document kind, not an in-place
499: edit.
500: 
501: ### Limits / 上限
502: 
503: Bounded at write time and re-checked at read time (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:53`):
504: 
505: | Bound | Value |
506: |---|---|
507: | whole file (writer **and** reader) | 1,048,576 B |
508: | plan / task rows | 128 |
509: | agent rows | 512 |
510: | stage rows | 16 |
511: | evidence rows | 1,024 |
512: | recorded attempts per task | 0–16 |
513: | objective / min-context objective | 4,000 chars |
514: | task title, acceptance criterion | 600 chars |
515: | error / failure reason, evidence claim | 1,000 chars |
516: | evidence locator | 400 chars |
517: | min-context digest | 12,000 chars (64 rows per section) |
518: | run id, session id | 120 chars |
519: | route label, branch name | 200 chars |
520: | declared write paths per task | 16 items × 300 chars |
521: | structural numbers (counts, timeouts) | 1,000,000 |
522: 
523: Overflow is handled three ways and they must not be confused: free **text** is truncated
524: with an explicit ellipsis marker (so the file is always writable), a **count** above a
525: ceiling is a hard `invalid` refusal, and a **whole file** above 1 MiB is `too-large` in both
526: directions — the writer refuses before touching the disk and the reader `stat`s first, so a
527: hostile or torn file is never parsed (`src/checkpoint/writer.ts:75`, `:132`).
528: 
529: Limits *observed in a run* are recorded, not policed: the schema stores whatever `limits`
530: the run actually used, and `limitContractViolations` only reports `maxConcurrency > 6` /
531: `maxRetries > 3` against the AGENTS.md envelope (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:105`, `:845`).
532: The configuration now matches that envelope exactly — defaults `maxConcurrency: 3` /
533: `maxRetries: 1`, hard caps `6` / `3` (`src/config.ts:22`) — so a checkpoint of a default
534: run records no violation. The former wider defaults (`4` / `2`, caps `1_000_000` / `10`)
535: are why the read side stays lenient: a file written by an older build must still load,
536: and `limitContractViolations` is how a caller reports one that is out of envelope.
537: 
538: Two ceilings, deliberately different: `countCeiling` (1,000,000) bounds structural counts,
539: while `msCeiling` (604,800,000 = 7 days) bounds durations and timeouts so that any
540: `HARD_LIMITS.timeoutMs` the plugin accepts stays recordable (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:95`,
541: `:101`; `src/config.ts:14`). The wiring adds a second rule on top of that: a deadline above the
542: recording ceiling is **omitted, never clamped** — `deadlineMs: 1000000` for a week-long run
543: would be a number describing no real bound — and the same value gates `time.deadlineAtMs` and
544: the derived `watchdog.deadlineHit` (`src/checkpoint/wiring.ts:455`).
545: 
546: Wiring's own bounds are about *rate* and *retention*, never content
547: (`src/checkpoint/wiring.ts:76`): a periodic rewrite every 1–300 s (default 30 s, timer
548: `unref()`ed so a checkpoint never keeps the process alive), at most 3 consecutive failed
549: writes before that run's recorder stops retrying, at most 4 remembered run ids per recorder,
550: and a 3 s bound on the unload write (an abandoned write is dropped, never retried).
551: 
552: Cleanup may never mask the coded refusal: both `catch` blocks in `writeCheckpoint` swallow a
553: failing `rm` (`src/checkpoint/writer.ts:91`, `:97`), so a caller that hits a bad path receives
554: `CheckpointError('io')` rather than a raw filesystem error. That property regressed once during
555: this round (a bare `rm` replaced the coded error on the `ENOTDIR` path) and is now pinned by
556: `test/checkpoint-schema.spec.ts` — see `docs/knowledge/VALIDATION.md` Round 38.
557: 
558: ### Refusals / 拒绝语义
559: 
560: Run-document side — `CheckpointError.reason` is exactly one of
561: `invalid | too-large | integrity | io` (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:296`):
562: 
563: - `invalid` — the object does not satisfy the schema (missing section, wrong type,
564:   `plan.taskCount` ≠ `plan.tasks.length`, count above a ceiling).
565: - `too-large` — the canonical payload or the file on disk exceeds 1 MiB.
566: - `integrity` — the recomputed sha-256 over the canonical payload (or its byte count) does
567:   not match the stored `integrity` record: the bytes were modified or torn after sealing.
568: - `io` — stat/read/write/rename failed, or the path is not a regular file.
569: 
570: Restore-document side — `RefusalReason` is exactly one of
571: `version-mismatch | corruption | conflict` (`src/resume/validator.ts:50`):
572: 
573: - `corruption` — unparsable JSON, wrong `kind`, missing or invalid digest, malformed record,
574:   bad field type, or a digest that no longer matches the body.
575: - `version-mismatch` — sealed with a format version this build does not restore.
576: - `conflict` — structurally intact and correctly sealed, yet its claims contradict the
577:   restore contract: unknown task status, duplicate task id, duplicate seq, or a `runId`
578:   other than the one the caller pinned.
579: 
580: Both sides fail closed: `evaluateResumeCheckpoint` refuses with the validator's reason and
581: never returns a plan (`src/resume/policy.ts:168`), so corruption, a foreign version, or a
582: wrong run can never trigger an automatic restore.
583: 
584: Recording never fails a run. Every write goes through `writeCheckpoint`, and a refusal
585: (`invalid` / `too-large` / `integrity` / `io`) is counted and logged as a warning, never
586: propagated into the work being recorded; after 3 consecutive failures the recorder stops
587: retrying that run, so a read-only or full disk costs one warning rather than one per tick
588: (`src/checkpoint/wiring.ts:47`, `:754`). The unload path bounds itself to 3 s and logs
589: `checkpoint unload hook failed: …` instead of blocking disposal (`src/run.ts:309`).
590: 
591: Retention is the other half of that policy: exactly five journaled states are retained —
592: `completed`, `interrupted`, `failed`, `gated`, `evidence-incomplete` — with their outputs,
593: files and evidence carried over verbatim, while a bare `success` mark is **never** retained
594: because a self-report is not verification; that task goes back to the planner
595: (`src/resume/policy.ts:35`, `:95`). Restore therefore never re-runs completed work and never
596: discards what an interrupted attempt already produced.
597: 
598: ### What the user sees / 用户可见面
599: 
600: Since **0.8.0**: a run writes `checkpoint-<runId>.json` under
601: `~/.dsh/checkpoints/grok-workflow` (or `$DSH_HOME` / `GROK_WORKFLOW_CHECKPOINT_DIR`) — one file
602: rewritten every 30 s, a terminal one at the end, and one `cancelled` shape on plugin unload.
603: There is **no restore UI, no resume button, no setting** and no line in a normal report: the
604: only trace a user could notice is a `logger.warn` line when a write fails. `resumeDecision`
605: answers a *host* question — "should a new run start from this file, and with which unfinished
606: tasks?" — in a reason string, and never claims engine-level resume: the shipped engine
607: journals nothing (stated limitation), so `resume` here means starting a new run that
608: re-drives the unfinished tasks from the recorded context. Two consequences belong in the same breath, because they are what a reader
609: will actually meet: **nothing prunes the directory** (one file per run id, rewritten in place
610: while the run lives, never deleted — the cost of retention is the user's disk), and **nothing
611: consumes the files** (`resumeDecision` has no production caller; `src/resume/` is imported only
612: by tests). The UX commitments an integration inherits:
613: 
614: 1. A refused restore is spoken out loud with its reason and detail — the same rule the gate
615:    already follows for refused messages (see `## Mandatory entry (the gate)`). Silence is not
616:    an acceptable outcome for "we found a checkpoint but would not use it".
617: 2. Restore is never silent or automatic: a *plan* is the only thing the policy produces, and
618:    it names each task's action (`retain` / `redrive` / `reverify` / `replan`), so a reader can
619:    see what would be kept and what would run again.
620: 3. The `detail` strings are written to be shown to a human verbatim (they name the offending
621:    field and value), so the failure path needs no separate copy.
622: 4. Checkpoints hold no secrets: every free-text field is redacted at build time through
623:    `src/redact.ts` (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:33`), which is also what makes a checkpoint
624:    safe to attach to an Issue.
625: 
626: ## Credential redaction (`src/redact.ts`)
627: 
628: One ordered rule table, applied to every model-facing report, diagnostic, checkpoint field,
629: and prompt-side worker output. `src/script.ts` renders the same table into the workflow
630: script (`redactionRulesSource`), so a rule added here protects both boundaries; the parity
631: test compares the two implementations over one corpus.
632: 
633: Covered shapes, in table order:
634: 
635: 1. `PRIVATE KEY` blocks — PEM and PGP armor (`BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK`) — replaced whole.
636: 2. Provider tokens by prefix: JWT, `sk-`/`rk-`/`pk-`, `ghp_`/`github_pat_`, `glpat-`, `npm_`,
637:    `xox*`, `AKIA`/`ASIA`, `AIza`, `ya29.`, Telegram bot tokens, Slack webhooks.
638: 3. `Cookie` / `Set-Cookie` header values — including the form written inside a quoted shell
639:    argument (`curl -H 'Cookie: …'`), where the header is not at the start of a line. The value
640:    stops at the closing quote so the rest of the command survives.
641: 4. `Bearer` and `Basic` authorization, header or JSON form.
642: 5. URL-borne credentials: `userinfo` in any scheme, and signature query parameters — `sig`,
643:    `signature`, `sharedaccesssignature`, `X-Amz-Signature`, `X-Goog-Signature`, `auth` — plus
644:    the `token`/`key`/`secret` query family. The signature alone grants access, so a presigned
645:    URL is a bearer credential.
646: 6. Secret-named assignments (`token`, `password`, `SECRET_KEY`, `client_secret`, …) in JSON,
647:    env and quoted form. By name in `redactDeep`, whose key normalisation treats `x-api-key`
648:    and `accessToken` alike.
649: 
650: Two deliberate asymmetries:
651: 
652: - **Under-redaction is a leak, over-redaction is noise.** A value that continues into a call
653:   (`refreshToken()`), a comparison (`password == null`) or a code keyword (`await`) is not
654:   redacted at all: rewriting source costs more than the missed shape, because the rewrite is
655:   itself reported as fact.
656: - **A value ends at a token boundary** — whitespace, end of line, or one of `,;}&|<>})]`. An
657:   unterminated value used to swallow `;user=app` and `Path=/` from the same line.
658: 
659: Known gaps: base64-wrapped PEM has no rule, and no list of shapes is complete. Redaction is a
660: safety net, not a guarantee (see the README security section).
661: 
662: ## Known architecture limits (MVP)
663: 
664: - No pause/resume, journaling, or cross-process resume. Checkpoints are written (see above),
665:   but the engine journals nothing: `resumeDecision` is a host-side decision over a file, not an
666:   engine restart, and no code path re-enters a run from one.
667: - No background job mode; the tool runs in the foreground and uses `exec.signal`.
668: - Model routing is **script-level (L1) only**: each call passes
669:   `{ provider, model }` from the role's chain, but the plugin does not register
670:   `agent/request`/`agent/request-error` consumers, so host-level (L2) rerouting
671:   and any interaction with `dsh-llm-retry` stay out of scope (decision U-2).
672: - No dependency graph between tasks; tasks are independent by design.
673: - Verification is independent-agent plus evidence validation, not a formal
674:   proof of correctness.
675: - All child agents in one workflow share the DSH session `cwd`. Parallel
676:   workers/verifiers are not filesystem-isolated; concurrent writers can
677:   clobber each other and a verifier can see another task's partial state.
678:   Declaration-driven mitigation exists (`writesPaths`, DESIGN DD-8a): tasks whose
679:   declared paths overlap are serialized. It is a mitigation, not a sandbox —
680:   a task that writes outside its declaration is invisible to the scheduler, so
681:   keep write scopes disjoint or set `maxConcurrency: 1` for write-heavy work.

(End of file - total 681 lines)

lines.text: # Architecture
## Goal
`dsh-grok-workflow` adds two things to DSH, using only documented capabilities:
a model-facing tool, `grok_workflow`, that turns a complex objective into a
bounded, verifiable multi-subagent workflow; and — since `0.2.0`, on by default —
an **entry gate** on `agent/pre-step` that makes that workflow mandatory for user
messages instead of opt-in. It does not implement a new agent loop, model
adapter, sandbox, or subagent runtime.
## Reused DSH capabilities
| Capability | DSH package/service | How this plugin uses it |

| Workflow execution | `ctx.workflowEngine` (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow`) via `src/team-engine.ts` | Starts a generated plain-JavaScript orchestration script; awaits `run.result`; always disposes. For task-team runs the engine is a private twin of the runtime's own PTC engine whose `subagents` view derives each child's durable display label from its prompt's first line; on any non-PTC engine the injected engine is used unchanged. |
| Script sandbox and child fan-out | `@deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow-ptc` | Executes the script in DSH's PTC runtime; `agent()` delegates to subagents. |
| Subagent lifecycle | `ctx.subagents` (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent`) | Provides child admission, cancellation, structured output, and teardown through the engine. |
| Tool registration | `ctx.tools` (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools`) | Registers `grok_workflow` with typed parameters and a JSON canonical result. |
| Prompt guidance | `ctx.systemPrompt` | Adds a short usage section explaining when the tool applies. |
| Plugin lifecycle | Cordis effects and `ctx.effect()` | Unregisters the tool/prompt and disposes active workflow runs on unload. |
| Profile installation | DSH bundle/profile patch layers | The bundle inserts one plugin row; disabling/removing the bundle removes the plugin. |
## Borrowed Grok Build strategy
Grok Build's deep-research workflow establishes a useful pattern:
1. **Plan** a small set of independent questions, bounded by breadth.
2. **Execute** structured research jobs in parallel.
3. **Verify** claims independently, validating exact IDs and rejecting malformed
verifier output.
4. **Synthesize** a report whose status is partial when coverage or verification
is incomplete.
This plugin adopts the strategy and the fail-closed evidence discipline, not
the implementation. Grok Build's Rhai scripts, Rust manager, journal, budget
leases, and pause/resume statuses are not ported. DSH's workflow engine already
provides sandboxed script execution, bounded child counts, cancellation, and
cleanup; the plugin adds the domain-specific plan/verify/retry/report policy.
## Execution design
```text
grok_workflow tool call
v
validate objective + optional caller-supplied tasks
v
build a static JS workflow script + args JSON
v
ctx.workflowEngine.start({ script, meta, args, parent, signal })
+--> Plan: planner agent (if no tasks supplied) with JSON schema
+--> Execute + Verify + Retry: bounded worker pool
|       for each task:
|         worker agent -> structured execution result
|         verifier agent -> criterion evidence
|         supervisor agent (serial) -> can only fail the attempt, never pass it
|         if failed and attempts remain: worker retry -> verifier
+--> Resident parallel supervision (host side, `src/guardian.ts`):
|       one `RunGuardian` per run, created before the engine starts and
|       adopted with the live run. It observes only
|       `workflow/agent-start` / `workflow/agent-end` / `workflow/end`,
|       judges liveness (never quality), and on a stall
|       (per-child timeout or run-wide heartbeat loss) cancels the run
|       at most once and records a bounded `Guardian` finding that the
|       terminal path folds into the report's errors. It never calls the
|       engine's `agent()` hook: zero model calls, no new agent role.
|       See `docs/knowledge/RESEARCH.md` A29 and `DECISIONS.md` D-074.
+--> Synthesize: deterministic host/script report
v
redact credentials recursively -> tool canonical JSON -> text render
The script is static; the objective, caller tasks, and limits cross the sandbox
as `args` JSON data. No user text is interpolated into code.
### Plan
The planner returns object-rooted structured output:
- `id`, `title`, `objective`, `expectedOutput`
- `acceptanceCriteria` (non-empty list)
- `context`, `constraints`
- optional `dependsOn` is intentionally rejected in the MVP: tasks must be
independent so concurrency and partial status are well-defined.
Host/script validation enforces unique IDs, non-empty required fields, at most
`maxTasks` tasks, no dependency graph, a **32,000-character workflow objective**,
and a 48,000-character aggregate serialized task budget. Each task's own
`objective`, `expectedOutput`, and `context` stay capped at 4,000 characters

(`taskTextChars`) — those task-level limits are unchanged. A planner failure or invalid plan falls back to segmented tasks covering the original objective verbatim: the objective is split into contiguous segments of at most 4,000 characters (`taskTextChars`), as close to equal as the bound allows and cut on a nearby paragraph, sentence or word break, concatenating the segment objectives reproduces the original byte for byte, every segment carries the same `origin_goal_id`, and the segment count follows the splitter (`src/shards.ts`) rather than `maxTasks`; the report records `planning.source: "fallback"` and cannot claim fully clean completion.
`acceptanceCriteria` is a non-empty list whose entries must stay distinct under
the comparison used to match a verifier's answer: trailing sentence punctuation,
collapsed whitespace, and letter case are ignored. A task whose criteria collide
after that normalization is rejected (host input validation and planner output
alike) because two criteria that compare equal cannot each be confirmed by
exactly one verifier entry. This makes some inputs that were previously accepted
invalid, for example `["Do X.", "do x"]` or `["alpha works", "alpha works!"]`;
write each requirement once, with distinct wording.
### Execute
Tasks run through a bounded worker pool implemented in the script. The pool size
is `maxConcurrency` (default 3, hard maximum 6). The script calls `agent()`
only from a pool worker, so at most that many child agents are in flight.
`maxTotalAgents` is also passed to the engine as a second backstop.
### Per-route concurrency: overflow, not fallback
Each route in a role's chain may carry an optional `maxInFlight` (1–64, blank =
unlimited). The counter is per route **inside one workflow run**: while a capped route is full,
a new call overflows to the next untried route in chain order instead of waiting
on the full one. Only when every untried route is full does the call wait for a
drain, and the wait is recorded as `queuedMs`. Counters live in the generated
script's per-run state and are never shared across runs, so a `Route overflows …`
entry can only ever describe yielding inside the run that produced it. Blank =
unlimited = never yields: a chain whose routes are all blank can never overflow.
A full lane is never a failure: it advances no fallback, costs no retry attempt,
and leaves the failure policy (`switchOn`) untouched. The distinction is visible
where it matters — the child's trail entry carries `skippedBusy` (which lanes
were yielded) and `queuedMs`, rendered as `Route overflows …` (separate from
`Route switches:`) and kept in the routing ledger — so "used route B because
route A was full" never reads as "route A failed".
### Verify
Every worker result is followed by a fresh verifier agent that receives the
task and the worker's structured result. The verifier must:
- inspect actual files/commands/sources rather than accept the worker summary;
- return one criterion result per acceptance criterion with non-empty evidence;
- return at least one concrete checked-evidence item;
- mark `pass` only when every criterion is met.
The host validates these conditions. A malformed or evidence-free `pass` is
converted to a failed verification and triggers a bounded retry.
### Supervise (two layers, orthogonal)
Supervision answers two different questions in two different places:
- **Serial supervisor (quality):** after verification and before synthesis, one
`supervisor` agent call per task attempt — but only when a supervisor chain
is configured. It can only fail an attempt, never pass one: a verifier
failure stands even when supervision passes. This is the D-056 semantic and
it is unchanged.
- **Resident parallel guardian (liveness):** one `RunGuardian` per run, alive
from before the engine starts until the run settles (`src/guardian.ts`). It
observes only `workflow/agent-start` / `workflow/agent-end` /
`workflow/end`, judges whether children are still alive (never what they
said), and on a stall — a per-child timeout or a run-wide heartbeat loss
against a budget derived from the run's own deadline (`min(deadline, 600s)`,
disarmed for `timeoutMs: 0`) — cancels the run at most once and records a
bounded `Guardian` finding that the terminal path folds into the report's
errors without changing its status. It never calls the engine's `agent()`
hook: zero model calls, no new agent role, no second scheduler. Plugin
unload disposes every live guardian with the runs it watches, so no timer,
listener, or registry entry outlives the unload. See `RESEARCH.md` A29 and
`DECISIONS.md` D-074.
One sentence: the supervisor answers "is the work right", the guardian
answers "is the work still alive".
### Retry
Each task has at most `maxRetries` retries after the initial attempt (default 1,
hard maximum 3). Retry attempts receive the prior result and verifier issues.
Attempt counts are reported; failures are never collapsed into success.
### Synthesize
The final report contains:
- `status`: `completed`, `partial`, or `failed`
- original objective and plan (source + tasks)
- per-task execution, verification, attempts, and errors
- confirmed findings/evidence
- incomplete items, errors, and uncertainties
- applied limits
Status rules:
- `completed` only when every planned task is verified and no planning fallback
or unresolved failure exists. A fallback or unavailable plan can never be
`completed`.
- `partial` when at least one task is verified but the workflow is not fully
clean, or when planning degraded to fallback. A fallback plan whose shards
verify successfully is still `partial`; the report keeps the fallback
provenance and the planning error. For non-fallback plans, `partial` requires
a mix of verified and failed tasks.
- `failed` when no task is verified.
## Lifecycle and cancellation
- The tool passes `exec.signal` to the workflow engine and also maps a
configurable deadline to `run.cancel()`.
- Every `execute` path awaits `run.result` and calls `run.dispose()` in
`finally`; partial output is never presented as success.
- The plugin tracks live runs in a `Set`. A plugin-level `ctx.effect()` aborts
its controller and disposes every live run during unload, then returns after
cleanup settles.
- Tool and prompt registrations are Cordis effects, so unload removes them.
- The resident guardian owns one `unref()`ed 1-second interval per live run
plus its three engine-event listeners and its instance-registry entry; all
three are released on `finish()`/`dispose()`, and `disposeActiveState`
disposes every live guardian with the runs it watches.
- There are no other plugin-owned timers, sockets, or listeners beyond the effect
cleanup and the deadline timer, which is cleared on every path.
## Registration and composition
The bundle patch inserts one row:
```yaml
- insert:
- id: grok-workflow
name: dsh-grok-workflow
The plugin exports `name`, `inject`, `Config`, and `apply`. It requires
`tools`, `workflowEngine`, and `systemPrompt`; the DSH base/web/headless
compositions provide the workflow engine and a subagent provider (`spawn`).
If they are absent, the plugin remains pending/fails loudly rather than
silently degrading.
### Settings surface
The exported `Config` schema is the settings surface. DSH's `ctx.settings`
(`SettingsForms`) projects every Loader entry's own schema into a form keyed by
the entry id (`grok-workflow`), reports `applies: 'live'` and `autoGenerate`
(default true), and writes edits through `update`/`replace`/`mutate` with a
revision check (`SETTINGS_CONFLICT`) into the profile patch file. The plugin
declares `ctx.settings.configure({ auto: true })` in `apply()` (soft failure on
runtimes without the hook) and validates its own configuration at load:
unknown keys are refused, `configVersion` is bounded, and every configured
route — all five routed roles, `supervisor` included, since its route is read
from the same table and it runs per task after that task's verifier — is checked
against `llm.listProviders()` plus, where the provider enumerates them, its
declared model ids. Nothing here is decorative: the
generated fields are the fields `resolveConfig()` reads. A bespoke chain editor
with model dropdowns would be a client-half package (`dsh.client`), not a core
change (see ROADMAP §9.2).
### Recoverable vs irrecoverable configuration (P1)
Only two configuration shapes are **recoverable** — a `synthesis` /
`roles.synthesizer` mismatch whose intent is unambiguous:
| # | Raw shape | Effective value | Log |
| (a) | synthesizer chain non-empty + `synthesis: deterministic` | `model` | `warn` names `model` + `已按 model 生效，请在设置页确认` |
| (b) | `synthesis: model` + empty synthesizer chain | `deterministic` | `warn` names `deterministic` + `已按 deterministic 生效，请在设置页确认` |
Mechanism: `repairSynthesisInconsistency(raw)` in `src/config.ts` is a pure
function — it returns `{ repaired, warnings[] }`, mutates nothing, validates
nothing, and matches only the two shapes above (anything else returns
unchanged with no warnings). `apply()` in `src/index.ts` calls
`reader.read()` at load as before; only when that throws does it snapshot the
raw config, run the repair, and re-resolve the repaired shape. The repaired
shape must itself resolve cleanly before any warning is emitted — so a second,
non-repairable defect behind the mismatch still fails hard. A repaired config
activates normally (tool + gate + settings surface all start) and carries
`synthesisRepaired: true`, which `describeResolvedConfig()` renders as
`synthesis=<mode> (repaired)` so the load log is self-proving. The same
fallback runs on every later `readConfig()`, so a bad settings save repairs
the same way. The run-time gate path (`gate.safe()` / `lastGood` in
`src/gate.ts`) is untouched.
Everything else is **irrecoverable** and still fails hard at load (R-06):
unknown keys, `configVersion` out of range, `gateScope: preset` without a
preset name, out-of-range numbers, malformed/duplicated/over-long chains,
unknown providers, models the provider enumerates but does not declare,
unknown `switchOn` classes, and budget-backstop violations. The settings page
mirrors the recoverable pair client-side (`src/client/index.js` `validate()`):
chain non-empty + deterministic, or `model` + empty chain, is a red
`error.synthesisChainUnused` / `error.synthesisChainMissing` finding (both
languages) that disables Save; only a legal combination may be written.
## Mandatory entry (the gate)
user message ──► agent/pre-step ──► classify
├─ not ours (subagent, non-user source, empty batch, out of scope, already routed) ──► pass through
├─ unusable (empty text, over 32000 chars) ──► refuse out loud, nothing runs
└─ admit ──► run the workflow ──► deliver the validated report in this turn
- **Classification is a whitelist** (`src/gate.ts`): only `source.kind === 'user'`
messages for the scoped agents are claimed. Subagent prompts, team messages,
webhooks, schedules, user-question replies and empty batches pass through — a
gate that claims everything would recurse.
- **Claiming is recorded, not guessed.** A per-message delivery record is written
into the session, so a re-dispatched batch cannot start a second run and an
interrupted delivery is not silently re-run.
- **Delivery is in-turn by default.** The turn stays open, the report is entered
as the step's message, and the main model finalises it in the same turn. The
alternatives (`relay`, `append`) deliver after the turn closes and therefore
need a long-lived surface.
- **A triage-team message on an interactive surface speaks first, then works in
the background (`receipt-then-relay`).** The pre-step writes one live first
answer into the turn (one light model call over the `triageModel` route; the
information structure is fixed, the wording is composed fresh every time, and
a failed call degrades to a plainly-labelled template fallback), then admits
the workflow into the per-agent queue; the result is delivered by `relay`
when it settles and the progress board stays live meanwhile. Anything that
cannot deliver in the background — headless one-shot (no `followup` turn),
`full` mode, a full queue, or any throw inside the interactive path — falls
back to the blocking `in-turn` run, so the final answer is never lost. The
`answerStrategy` configured value is unchanged (`in-turn` default); what
changed is the triage-team walk on a surface that can deliver later.
Cancelling is whole-round: a new message for the same session cancels the
in-flight run (`run.cancel` + `commitCancelled`) and restarts narrowed
(`carriedPendingRequest` / `resumedTarget`); V1 offers no subtask-level
redirect.
- **The gate reads the live configuration** on every decision (holders, see the
settings section), so an edit applies to the next message while an in-flight
run keeps its snapshot; an invalid edit refuses that message with its reason
and delivery falls back to the last good snapshot.
- **Failure modes are bounded:** the queue per agent is capped
(`maxQueuedMessages`), the run is bounded (`maxActiveRuns`, `timeoutMs`), and a
broken configuration is reported rather than swallowed.
### Objective length boundary
The objective limit is defined once as `TASK_LIMITS.objectiveChars` (`32_000`)
in `src/input.ts`, mirrored by the generated script in `src/script.ts`, and
enforced on the gate path (`src/gate.ts`), the direct `grok_workflow` tool call
(`src/index.ts`), and `composeObjective()` (`src/history.ts`).
| User message length | Gate (`agent/pre-step`) | Direct tool call | Result |
| 4,000 characters | admit | accept | run starts; the whole message is kept |
| 4,001 characters | admit | accept | run starts; the whole message is kept |
| 32,000 characters | admit | accept | run starts; the `Current request:` label is dropped and no history is attached, so the objective is exactly 32,000 characters |
| 32,001 characters | refuse | reject | no run starts; the refusal names the 32,000-character limit |
Every length from 4,001 through 32,000 characters is admitted; 32,001 is the
first refused length.
`composeObjective()` never shortens the current message. It returns `undefined`
only when the message itself exceeds the limit; when the 17-character
`Current request:\n` label would push the composed objective over the limit, it
returns the message unchanged instead of trimming it. Only the history block is
truncated. `historyChars` (default 20,000, hard maximum 1,000,000) and
`taskTextChars` (4,000 per task field) are unchanged.
**Planner-failure fallback.** When planning fails, `fallbackPlan()` splits the
whole objective into contiguous segments of at most `taskTextChars` characters;
concatenating the segment objectives reproduces the original objective byte for
byte. The segments are as close to equal as the bound allows — a 4,001-character
objective becomes two ~2,000-character segments, never a 4,000-character one plus
a one-character stub — and a cut that lands near a paragraph break, a sentence end
or a word break is moved onto it, so a segment ends where the text already ends.
Every segment carries the same `origin_goal_id`, so the fallback is traceable to
the one original goal, and each segment's acceptance criterion names the segment
it covers, so a verifier confirms the piece it was handed and no shard stands in
for the whole objective. `src/shards.ts` is the single implementation of that
split: the generated script runs it, and host validation re-derives the expected
segments with it and rejects a fallback plan carrying anything else. The segment
count therefore follows the splitter — not `maxTasks`, and not
`ceil(objectiveChars / taskTextChars)` either, because a boundary that backs off a
surrogate pair adds a segment. Host validation accepts a fallback plan over the
configured task cap (a fallback must not be rejected a second time) while still
enforcing the per-task text bound, and it does not apply the authored-text
aggregate budget to the fallback: that budget bounds task text a planner or caller
wrote, and the fallback's text is the caller's own objective, whose JSON escaping
can inflate the serialized plan past the budget without adding a character of
work. The run reports `partial` with `planning.source: "fallback"` and the
planner error.
## Non-interference
When the bundle is not installed or its row is disabled:
- no tool is registered;
- no prompt section is added;
- no `agent/pre-step` listener exists, so no message is claimed;
- no workflow runs exist;
- ordinary DSH sessions behave exactly as before.
Setting `enforceGate: false` keeps the tool and drops the listener, which is the
`0.1.0` behaviour.
## CI versus local-only tests
CI can run:
- TypeScript typecheck, lint, unit tests with a fake workflow engine and fake
agent boundary;
- engine contract tests (`test/engine-contract.spec.ts`) that run the generated
script against the **real** `@deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow-ptc` engine with a fake
subagent provider — the real `dsh-ptc-runtime`, `dsh-sandbox`, `dsh-scope`,
`dsh-session` and `dsh-workflow-ptc` devDependencies exist for that suite, not
for the published plugin;
- mandatory-entry tests (`test/gate.spec.ts`, `test/history.spec.ts`) that drive
`agent/pre-step` through a fake agent boundary, including the refusal paths;
- composition tests (`test/composition.spec.ts`) that dispatch `agent/pre-step`
through a **real cordis waterfall** shared with faithful reproductions of the
in-tree listeners (provenance in `test/composition-listeners.ts`), so the
ordering, `prepend` placement and veto semantics are the runtime's own;
- build and package-content checks;
- a Loader integration test using the real DSH Loader and real DSH tool
registry, with only the subagent boundary faked.
CI cannot prove a real model-produced workflow, a real DSH UI session, or that the
in-tree reproductions still match the installed DSH; re-run the audit command in
`docs/knowledge/PRE-STEP-COMPOSITION.md` after a DSH upgrade.
Those must be run locally with a real DSH profile and are recorded separately
as local runtime evidence.
For the delivery path there is one local check worth running after any change to
`answerStrategy`, the gate, or the DSH version:
```bash
npm run build
E2E_MODEL_PATCH=scripts/e2e-model-patch.yml scripts/e2e-headless-in-turn.sh
It boots one real `dsh headless` turn with this plugin overlaid by file URL (nothing is
installed into a profile) and fails unless the validated report actually reaches the user
in that single turn. The `in-turn` timing itself needs no model and is covered in CI by
the `in-turn delivery` suite in `test/gate.spec.ts`.
Two variants are worth knowing:
```bash
# a message the gate refuses on purpose must be refused OUT LOUD, with no run
E2E_EXPECT=refusal E2E_PROMPT="$(cat /tmp/over-32000-chars.txt)" \
E2E_MODEL_PATCH=scripts/e2e-model-patch.yml scripts/e2e-headless-in-turn.sh
`E2E_EXPECT=refusal` inverts the assertion: the refusal text (and its reason) must appear,
and no `Grok workflow:` status line and no task lines may appear — the user sees why nothing
ran instead of a silent no-op (V-2). The positive run is also the check that the real Loader
hands `.volatile()` configuration over as holders and the plugin unwraps them (DESIGN E-40).
## Checkpoint and resume (record + re-drive policy)
Status (since **0.8.0**): `src/checkpoint/` (schema, atomic writer,
engine wiring) and `src/resume/` (validator, restore policy) ship since **0.8.0** and are
exercised by `test/checkpoint-schema.spec.ts`, `test/checkpoint-wiring.spec.ts` and
`test/resume-validator.spec.ts`. The wiring *is* called: `src/run.ts` creates one recorder per
run, adopts it with the engine's run object and finalises it on the terminal path,
while `disposeActiveState` writes one `cancelled`
checkpoint per live run before it aborts. No user-visible surface changed — a run gains a JSON file on disk and, on
failure, a warning line. This section is the contract the code implements.
Boundary (D-013, measured on DSH **0.2.1-rc.2**; the install, activation and settings
projection of this bundle were re-verified on **0.2.2-rc.3** in RSI round 8, which did *not*
re-measure this journaling boundary): `resume` never means engine-level resume — the shipped
engine journals nothing and states it as a limitation. `resumeDecision` answers a host
question ("should a new run re-drive the unfinished tasks from this file?") and has had no
production caller since **0.8.0** (as of **0.11.9** `src/resume/` is imported only by tests).
Recording never terminates a run: recording is best-effort and unload-bounded, and a refused
disk costs a warning line, never the report. There is no Command Watchdog and no Host Evidence
Collector as of **0.11.9** (NOT_DONE, no implementation in the tree) — those names must not
appear as shipped features in release notes.
### Location / 位置
- The writer never chooses a directory: `writeCheckpoint(filePath, input)` takes the final
path from the caller and creates the parent directories (`src/checkpoint/writer.ts:71`).
- Filename policy is `checkpointFileName(runId)`: `checkpoint-<runId>.json`, every character
outside `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` replaced by `_`, truncated to `CHECKPOINT_LIMITS.idChars` (120),
and the degenerate `''` / `.` / `..` cases folded to `checkpoint-run.json`
(`src/checkpoint/writer.ts:59`). Filename derivation is total: any run id yields exactly
one safe name.
- Default directory (wiring): `checkpointDir()` resolves an explicit `options.dir`, then
`GROK_WORKFLOW_CHECKPOINT_DIR`, then `$DSH_HOME` (else `~/.dsh`) +
`checkpoints/grok-workflow` (`src/checkpoint/wiring.ts:125`), and `checkpointFile(runId)`
joins that with `checkpointFileName(runId)` (`:135`). The three-step shape is deliberately
the one the incremental memory archive already uses (`src/memory/archive.ts:141`). There is
**no setting** for it: the path is host state, not a display preference, so no configuration
key selects a policy — an integration that wants a different directory passes `dir` (or the
environment variable) at the call site.
### Version policy / 版本策略
Two independent versions, each refused rather than migrated:
- run document: `CHECKPOINT_VERSION = 'grok-workflow.checkpoint/v1'`
(`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:46`);
- restore document: `RESUME_CHECKPOINT_VERSION = 1` with envelope kind
`grok-workflow.resume-checkpoint` (`src/resume/validator.ts:28`).
The validator accepts exactly the version it was built with; anything else is
`version-mismatch` and restore is denied (`src/resume/validator.ts:208`). There is no
migration path and no "best effort" read: a checkpoint written by a newer build is refused
by an older one, by design. Bumping either number is a new document kind, not an in-place
edit.
### Limits / 上限
Bounded at write time and re-checked at read time (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:53`):
| Bound | Value |
| whole file (writer **and** reader) | 1,048,576 B |
| plan / task rows | 128 |
| agent rows | 512 |
| stage rows | 16 |
| evidence rows | 1,024 |
| recorded attempts per task | 0–16 |
| objective / min-context objective | 4,000 chars |
| task title, acceptance criterion | 600 chars |
| error / failure reason, evidence claim | 1,000 chars |
| evidence locator | 400 chars |
| min-context digest | 12,000 chars (64 rows per section) |
| run id, session id | 120 chars |
| route label, branch name | 200 chars |
| declared write paths per task | 16 items × 300 chars |
| structural numbers (counts, timeouts) | 1,000,000 |
Overflow is handled three ways and they must not be confused: free **text** is truncated
with an explicit ellipsis marker (so the file is always writable), a **count** above a
ceiling is a hard `invalid` refusal, and a **whole file** above 1 MiB is `too-large` in both
directions — the writer refuses before touching the disk and the reader `stat`s first, so a
hostile or torn file is never parsed (`src/checkpoint/writer.ts:75`, `:132`).
Limits *observed in a run* are recorded, not policed: the schema stores whatever `limits`
the run actually used, and `limitContractViolations` only reports `maxConcurrency > 6` /
`maxRetries > 3` against the AGENTS.md envelope (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:105`, `:845`).
The configuration now matches that envelope exactly — defaults `maxConcurrency: 3` /
`maxRetries: 1`, hard caps `6` / `3` (`src/config.ts:22`) — so a checkpoint of a default
run records no violation. The former wider defaults (`4` / `2`, caps `1_000_000` / `10`)
are why the read side stays lenient: a file written by an older build must still load,
and `limitContractViolations` is how a caller reports one that is out of envelope.
Two ceilings, deliberately different: `countCeiling` (1,000,000) bounds structural counts,
while `msCeiling` (604,800,000 = 7 days) bounds durations and timeouts so that any
`HARD_LIMITS.timeoutMs` the plugin accepts stays recordable (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:95`,
`:101`; `src/config.ts:14`). The wiring adds a second rule on top of that: a deadline above the
recording ceiling is **omitted, never clamped** — `deadlineMs: 1000000` for a week-long run
would be a number describing no real bound — and the same value gates `time.deadlineAtMs` and
the derived `watchdog.deadlineHit` (`src/checkpoint/wiring.ts:455`).
Wiring's own bounds are about *rate* and *retention*, never content
(`src/checkpoint/wiring.ts:76`): a periodic rewrite every 1–300 s (default 30 s, timer
`unref()`ed so a checkpoint never keeps the process alive), at most 3 consecutive failed
writes before that run's recorder stops retrying, at most 4 remembered run ids per recorder,
and a 3 s bound on the unload write (an abandoned write is dropped, never retried).
Cleanup may never mask the coded refusal: both `catch` blocks in `writeCheckpoint` swallow a
failing `rm` (`src/checkpoint/writer.ts:91`, `:97`), so a caller that hits a bad path receives
`CheckpointError('io')` rather than a raw filesystem error. That property regressed once during
this round (a bare `rm` replaced the coded error on the `ENOTDIR` path) and is now pinned by
`test/checkpoint-schema.spec.ts` — see `docs/knowledge/VALIDATION.md` Round 38.
### Refusals / 拒绝语义
Run-document side — `CheckpointError.reason` is exactly one of
`invalid | too-large | integrity | io` (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:296`):
- `invalid` — the object does not satisfy the schema (missing section, wrong type,
`plan.taskCount` ≠ `plan.tasks.length`, count above a ceiling).
- `too-large` — the canonical payload or the file on disk exceeds 1 MiB.
- `integrity` — the recomputed sha-256 over the canonical payload (or its byte count) does
not match the stored `integrity` record: the bytes were modified or torn after sealing.
- `io` — stat/read/write/rename failed, or the path is not a regular file.
Restore-document side — `RefusalReason` is exactly one of
`version-mismatch | corruption | conflict` (`src/resume/validator.ts:50`):
- `corruption` — unparsable JSON, wrong `kind`, missing or invalid digest, malformed record,
bad field type, or a digest that no longer matches the body.
- `version-mismatch` — sealed with a format version this build does not restore.
- `conflict` — structurally intact and correctly sealed, yet its claims contradict the
restore contract: unknown task status, duplicate task id, duplicate seq, or a `runId`
other than the one the caller pinned.
Both sides fail closed: `evaluateResumeCheckpoint` refuses with the validator's reason and
never returns a plan (`src/resume/policy.ts:168`), so corruption, a foreign version, or a
wrong run can never trigger an automatic restore.
Recording never fails a run. Every write goes through `writeCheckpoint`, and a refusal
(`invalid` / `too-large` / `integrity` / `io`) is counted and logged as a warning, never
propagated into the work being recorded; after 3 consecutive failures the recorder stops
retrying that run, so a read-only or full disk costs one warning rather than one per tick
(`src/checkpoint/wiring.ts:47`, `:754`). The unload path bounds itself to 3 s and logs
`checkpoint unload hook failed: …` instead of blocking disposal (`src/run.ts:309`).
Retention is the other half of that policy: exactly five journaled states are retained —
`completed`, `interrupted`, `failed`, `gated`, `evidence-incomplete` — with their outputs,
files and evidence carried over verbatim, while a bare `success` mark is **never** retained
because a self-report is not verification; that task goes back to the planner
(`src/resume/policy.ts:35`, `:95`). Restore therefore never re-runs completed work and never
discards what an interrupted attempt already produced.
### What the user sees / 用户可见面
Since **0.8.0**: a run writes `checkpoint-<runId>.json` under
`~/.dsh/checkpoints/grok-workflow` (or `$DSH_HOME` / `GROK_WORKFLOW_CHECKPOINT_DIR`) — one file
rewritten every 30 s, a terminal one at the end, and one `cancelled` shape on plugin unload.
There is **no restore UI, no resume button, no setting** and no line in a normal report: the
only trace a user could notice is a `logger.warn` line when a write fails. `resumeDecision`
answers a *host* question — "should a new run start from this file, and with which unfinished
tasks?" — in a reason string, and never claims engine-level resume: the shipped engine
journals nothing (stated limitation), so `resume` here means starting a new run that
re-drives the unfinished tasks from the recorded context. Two consequences belong in the same breath, because they are what a reader
will actually meet: **nothing prunes the directory** (one file per run id, rewritten in place
while the run lives, never deleted — the cost of retention is the user's disk), and **nothing
consumes the files** (`resumeDecision` has no production caller; `src/resume/` is imported only
by tests). The UX commitments an integration inherits:
1. A refused restore is spoken out loud with its reason and detail — the same rule the gate
already follows for refused messages (see `## Mandatory entry (the gate)`). Silence is not
an acceptable outcome for "we found a checkpoint but would not use it".
2. Restore is never silent or automatic: a *plan* is the only thing the policy produces, and
it names each task's action (`retain` / `redrive` / `reverify` / `replan`), so a reader can
see what would be kept and what would run again.
3. The `detail` strings are written to be shown to a human verbatim (they name the offending
field and value), so the failure path needs no separate copy.
4. Checkpoints hold no secrets: every free-text field is redacted at build time through
`src/redact.ts` (`src/checkpoint/schema.ts:33`), which is also what makes a checkpoint
safe to attach to an Issue.
## Credential redaction (`src/redact.ts`)
One ordered rule table, applied to every model-facing report, diagnostic, checkpoint field,
and prompt-side worker output. `src/script.ts` renders the same table into the workflow
script (`redactionRulesSource`), so a rule added here protects both boundaries; the parity
test compares the two implementations over one corpus.
Covered shapes, in table order:
1. `PRIVATE KEY` blocks — PEM and PGP armor (`BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK`) — replaced whole.
2. Provider tokens by prefix: JWT, `sk-`/`rk-`/`pk-`, `ghp_`/`github_pat_`, `glpat-`, `npm_`,
`xox*`, `AKIA`/`ASIA`, `AIza`, `ya29.`, Telegram bot tokens, Slack webhooks.
3. `Cookie` / `Set-Cookie` header values — including the form written inside a quoted shell
argument (`curl -H 'Cookie: …'`), where the header is not at the start of a line. The value
stops at the closing quote so the rest of the command survives.
4. `Bearer` and `Basic` authorization, header or JSON form.
5. URL-borne credentials: `userinfo` in any scheme, and signature query parameters — `sig`,
`signature`, `sharedaccesssignature`, `X-Amz-Signature`, `X-Goog-Signature`, `auth` — plus
the `token`/`key`/`secret` query family. The signature alone grants access, so a presigned
URL is a bearer credential.
6. Secret-named assignments (`token`, `password`, `SECRET_KEY`, `client_secret`, …) in JSON,
env and quoted form. By name in `redactDeep`, whose key normalisation treats `x-api-key`
and `accessToken` alike.
Two deliberate asymmetries:
- **Under-redaction is a leak, over-redaction is noise.** A value that continues into a call
(`refreshToken()`), a comparison (`password == null`) or a code keyword (`await`) is not
redacted at all: rewriting source costs more than the missed shape, because the rewrite is
itself reported as fact.
- **A value ends at a token boundary** — whitespace, end of line, or one of `,;}&|<>})]`. An
unterminated value used to swallow `;user=app` and `Path=/` from the same line.
Known gaps: base64-wrapped PEM has no rule, and no list of shapes is complete. Redaction is a
safety net, not a guarantee (see the README security section).
## Known architecture limits (MVP)
- No pause/resume, journaling, or cross-process resume. Checkpoints are written (see above),
but the engine journals nothing: `resumeDecision` is a host-side decision over a file, not an
engine restart, and no code path re-enters a run from one.
- No background job mode; the tool runs in the foreground and uses `exec.signal`.
- Model routing is **script-level (L1) only**: each call passes
`{ provider, model }` from the role's chain, but the plugin does not register
`agent/request`/`agent/request-error` consumers, so host-level (L2) rerouting
and any interaction with `dsh-llm-retry` stay out of scope (decision U-2).
- No dependency graph between tasks; tasks are independent by design.
- Verification is independent-agent plus evidence validation, not a formal
proof of correctness.
- All child agents in one workflow share the DSH session `cwd`. Parallel
workers/verifiers are not filesystem-isolated; concurrent writers can
clobber each other and a verifier can see another task's partial state.
Declaration-driven mitigation exists (`writesPaths`, DESIGN DD-8a): tasks whose
declared paths overlap are serialized. It is a mitigation, not a sandbox —
a task that writes outside its declaration is invisible to the scheduler, so
keep write scopes disjoint or set `maxConcurrency: 1` for write-heavy work.

1: # Release and Versioning / 版本与发布
2: 
3: This repository publishes source-based GitHub Releases; it is **not published to npm**. The release workflow validates a version tag, runs the full CI checks, extracts the matching bilingual changelog section, builds a package tarball, and creates a GitHub Release only if all checks pass.
4: 
5: 本项目通过 GitHub Releases 发布源码版本，**不发布到 npm**。发布工作流会校验版本标签、运行完整 CI 检查、提取对应的双语更新日志、打包插件，并且只有全部检查通过才会创建 GitHub Release。
6: 
7: ## What each record is for / 每类记录的作用
8: 
9: - **Git commits** are the source-code history and the first place to look when inspecting or reverting a change.
10: - **Git tags** such as `v0.1.1` point to a specific commit and are the stable version identifier.
11: - **GitHub Releases** display the bilingual changelog for a tag and attach the generated `.tgz` package.
12: - **CHANGELOG.md** records what users can expect in each version.
13: - These records are not a separate disaster-recovery backup. For protection against repository deletion or account loss, periodically clone/mirror the repository to another location. Back up local DSH configuration, credentials, and runtime data separately; never commit secrets.
14: 
15: - **Git 提交记录**保存源代码修改历史，排查问题或回退代码时优先查看。
16: - **Git 标签**（例如 `v0.1.1`）固定指向某个提交，是安装指定版本的依据。
17: - **GitHub Releases**展示该标签对应的双语更新日志，并附带生成的 `.tgz` 包。
18: - **CHANGELOG.md**记录各版本对用户的实际影响。
19: - 这些记录不等于独立的灾难恢复备份。为防止仓库被删除或账号丢失，应定期将仓库克隆或镜像到另一个位置。DSH 本地配置、凭据和运行数据需要单独备份，绝不能把密钥提交进仓库。

21: ## Version rule / 版本规则
22: 
23: Use Semantic Versioning with the form `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`:
24: 
25: | Change | Example | Rule |
26: |---|---|---|
27: | Bug fix or security fix, no intended breaking change | `0.1.0 → 0.1.1` | Increment PATCH |
28: | Backward-compatible feature | `0.1.1 → 0.2.0` | Increment MINOR |
29: | Breaking change | `0.2.0 → 1.0.0` | Increment MAJOR |
30: 
31: Every user-visible fix or feature should first be listed under `[Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md`. When preparing a release, move those entries into a versioned section and keep English and Simplified Chinese content in sync. A code commit does not automatically mean a new public version; publish a version after the change is reviewed and the checks pass.
32: 
33: 采用 `主版本.次版本.修订版本` 格式：
34: 
35: | 变更类型 | 示例 | 规则 |
36: |---|---|---|
37: | 不改变预期兼容性的 Bug / 安全修复 | `0.1.0 → 0.1.1` | 修订版本 +1 |
38: | 向后兼容的新功能 | `0.1.1 → 0.2.0` | 次版本 +1 |
39: | 不兼容的重大变更 | `0.2.0 → 1.0.0` | 主版本 +1 |
40: 
41: 每个用户可见的功能或修复，都应先写入 `CHANGELOG.md` 的 `[Unreleased]`。准备发布时，再把对应条目移入带版本号的章节，并同步英文和简体中文。一次代码提交不等于一次公开发版；需要先完成审查并通过检查，再发布版本。

lines.text: # Release and Versioning / 版本与发布

This repository publishes source-based GitHub Releases; it is **not published to npm**. The release workflow validates a version tag, runs the full CI checks, extracts the matching bilingual changelog section, builds a package tarball, and creates a GitHub Release only if all checks pass.
本项目通过 GitHub Releases 发布源码版本，**不发布到 npm**。发布工作流会校验版本标签、运行完整 CI 检查、提取对应的双语更新日志、打包插件，并且只有全部检查通过才会创建 GitHub Release。
## What each record is for / 每类记录的作用
- **Git commits** are the source-code history and the first place to look when inspecting or reverting a change.
- **Git tags** such as `v0.1.1` point to a specific commit and are the stable version identifier.
- **GitHub Releases** display the bilingual changelog for a tag and attach the generated `.tgz` package.
- **CHANGELOG.md** records what users can expect in each version.

- These records are not a separate disaster-recovery backup. For protection against repository deletion or account loss, periodically clone/mirror the repository to another location. Back up local DSH configuration, credentials, and runtime data separately; never commit secrets.
- **Git 提交记录**保存源代码修改历史，排查问题或回退代码时优先查看。
- **Git 标签**（例如 `v0.1.1`）固定指向某个提交，是安装指定版本的依据。
- **GitHub Releases**展示该标签对应的双语更新日志，并附带生成的 `.tgz` 包。
- **CHANGELOG.md**记录各版本对用户的实际影响。
- 这些记录不等于独立的灾难恢复备份。为防止仓库被删除或账号丢失，应定期将仓库克隆或镜像到另一个位置。DSH 本地配置、凭据和运行数据需要单独备份，绝不能把密钥提交进仓库。
## Version rule / 版本规则
Use Semantic Versioning with the form `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`:
| Change | Example | Rule |
| Bug fix or security fix, no intended breaking change | `0.1.0 → 0.1.1` | Increment PATCH |
| Backward-compatible feature | `0.1.1 → 0.2.0` | Increment MINOR |
| Breaking change | `0.2.0 → 1.0.0` | Increment MAJOR |

Every user-visible fix or feature should first be listed under `[Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md`. When preparing a release, move those entries into a versioned section and keep English and Simplified Chinese content in sync. A code commit does not automatically mean a new public version; publish a version after the change is reviewed and the checks pass.
采用 `主版本.次版本.修订版本` 格式：
| 变更类型 | 示例 | 规则 |
| 不改变预期兼容性的 Bug / 安全修复 | `0.1.0 → 0.1.1` | 修订版本 +1 |
每个用户可见的功能或修复，都应先写入 `CHANGELOG.md` 的 `[Unreleased]`。准备发布时，再把对应条目移入带版本号的章节，并同步英文和简体中文。一次代码提交不等于一次公开发版；需要先完成审查并通过检查，再发布版本。
## First version / 首次发版
`v0.1.0` was published on 2026-10-25 from commit `a7d5a62`; the release workflow run `40182751006` passed and created the GitHub Release with the package tarball.

`## [0.2.0] - 2026-10-26` 章节即为当时发布流程提取的文本。`0.2.1` 是它之上的增量版本，

## Publish a later version / 发布后续版本
1. Create a release branch and bump both `package.json` and `package-lock.json`. For a bug fix, for example, run:
```sh
npm version patch --no-git-tag-version
Use `npm version minor --no-git-tag-version` for a new compatible feature, or `major` for a breaking release.
2. Edit `CHANGELOG.md`: move the shipped entries from `[Unreleased]` into a new heading such as `## [0.1.1] - YYYY-MM-DD`; add a fresh `[Unreleased]` section and keep both languages synchronized.
3. Run the checks locally:
```sh
npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm run build
git diff --exit-code -- lib/
npm test
npm pack --dry-run
4. Commit these changes, open a PR, and merge only after review and green CI. From the updated `main`, tag and push the exact merged commit, for example:
```sh
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
git tag v0.1.1
git push origin v0.1.1
5. Open the Actions tab and check the Release workflow. It creates the GitHub Release and attaches the package tarball when all checks pass.

6. Do not move or overwrite a tag after a GitHub Release exists. If the first release validation fails before any Release is created, fix the workflow/source, delete and recreate the tag at the fixed commit, and record the move. After a Release exists, publish a new version instead. The release workflow currently runs on Node.js 22 only; main CI covers Node 22 and 24.

<type>file</type>
<content>
1: # Local Testing
2: 
3: ## Requirements
4: 
5: - Node.js 22+ (verified locally with Node 26.8.1)
6: - npm or pnpm
7: - DSH CLI `0.2.1-rc.2` (full runs) or `0.2.2-rc.3` (activation and settings projection, RSI
8:   round 8)
9: - A DSH profile with `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base` / `dsh-web-app` or
10:   `dsh-headless`; those bundles provide `workflow-ptc`, `subagent`, and the
11:   `spawn` provider.
12: 
13: ## Install dependencies and build
14: 
15: ```sh
16: npm install
17: npm run typecheck
18: npm run lint
19: npm test
20: npm run build
21: ```
22: 
23: `npm test` uses deterministic unit tests and a real DSH Loader integration
24: test with a fake subagent boundary. It does not call a model.
25: 
26: ## Install into a DSH profile (development mode)
27: 
28: From the repository parent directory, create the profile **before** installing
29: the plugin. `--from-default-profile` replaces profile content, so running it
30: after `plugin add` would remove the installed bundle:
31: 
32: ```sh
33: dsh --profile grok-workflow-dev --from-default-profile headless --dump-config
34: dsh plugin --profile grok-workflow-dev add /path/to/dsh-grok-workflow
35: dsh --profile grok-workflow-dev --dump-config | grep -n -A6 'grok-workflow'
36: ```
37: 
38: Replace `/path/to/dsh-grok-workflow` with the checkout path. The bundle is a
39: local checkout, so this is a development-mode install. It is not an npm
40: release.
41: 
42: ## Configuration
43: 
44: Configuration keys and their hard limits are listed in the
45: [README configuration table](../README.md#configuration-reference).
46: `0.11.14` accepts exactly thirteen keys (`toolName`, `mode`, `grokDefault`, `roles`,
47: `synthesis`, `maxConcurrency`, `maxTasks`, `timeoutMs`, `loopEnabled`,
48: `loopMaxRounds`, `loopFailStreak`, `loopIntervalMin`, `configVersion`);
49: everything else is fixed inside the plugin (`maxRetries=1`,
50: `maxActiveRuns=2` per session / `8` per process) and a patch that still carries
51: a removed key is rejected at load. `timeoutMs` defaults to `3600000` (60 min);
52: `0` means unlimited. Values are tightened by the calling profile,
53: not by editing this repository.
54: 
55: ## Enable
56: 
57: The bundle patch inserts the plugin row automatically, but **a row in the graph is
58: not an activated plugin**. The plugin injects `workflowEngine` (the seam owned by
59: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-workflow`), and that seam only exists while a workflow *provider*
60: row is active. `@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app` ships `workflow-ptc` with
61: `disabled: true`, so a stock web profile leaves this plugin **pending** forever:
62: `apply()` never runs, no `grok_workflow` tool is registered, no settings namespace
63: is served and no gate claims messages — while `--dump-config` still prints the row.
64: Measured on DSH 0.2.1-rc.2 in t32/t33 (see
65: [knowledge/VALIDATION.md](knowledge/VALIDATION.md)).
66: 
67: Verified activation, step by step (anyone can repeat it):
68: 
69: ```sh
70: # 1. profile (web app). `--from-default-profile` REPLACES content, so do it first.
71: dsh --profile grok-workflow-dev --from-default-profile web
72: 
73: # 2. install the packed plugin (adds the dependency AND the bundle row)
74: dsh plugin --profile grok-workflow-dev add ./dsh-grok-workflow-0.11.18.tgz
75: 
76: # 3. re-enable a workflow provider in the profile patch
77: #    <profile>/cordis.patch.yml:
78: #      - id: workflow-ptc
79: #        config: { provider: spawn }
80: #        disabled: false
81: 
82: # 4. start it (a new instance on its own port; never restart a running one)
83: dsh --profile grok-workflow-dev --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3199 --no-open
84: ```
85: 
86: Acceptance for "it is really active" (all four, in this order):
87: 
88: | Check | Expected |
89: | --- | --- |
90: | boot output | no `grok-workflow (...) pending` and no `did not activate` warning |
91: | `POST /api/settings/describe` | a namespace `grok-workflow` with `autoGenerate: true` |
92: | Plugins page (web GUI) | a card `Grok workflow`; opening it shows the settings page |
93: | a real session's `request/header.tools` | contains `grok_workflow` |
94: 
95: Verified again on `0.2.2-rc.3` (RSI round 8, 2026-11-18): a fresh profile created from the
96: `web` template, `dsh plugin add` of this checkout (installed as a `link:` dependency), the
97: `workflow-ptc` row re-enabled, then a boot on `127.0.0.1:3199` whose only output was the URL
98: line — no `pending` row and no `did not activate` warning — and a settings projection with 23
99: namespaces, one of them `grok-workflow` with `autoGenerate: true`. The model-backed message
100: was not run: see "Real-model smoke" for the `MISSING_CREDENTIAL` line.
101: 
102: Three traps that cost real time in t32 (all reproduced):
103: 
104: - **A stale install.** `dsh plugin add` with the *same* `file:` tarball path is a
105:   pnpm no-op: the profile keeps the previously installed contents (the manifest
106:   said `dsh` without `client`, and the new `lib/client.js` was missing). Add a
107:   freshly named copy (`cp …-0.11.5.tgz /tmp/g$(date +%s%N).tgz`) or change the
108:   version, then confirm the installed `node_modules/<pkg>/package.json`.
109: - **`plugin add` rewrites the bundle list.** After adding a second package the
110:   profile's `dsh.profile.bundles` contained only that package — the earlier
111:   third-party bundle had been dropped. Re-add every bundle or edit
112:   `dsh.profile.bundles` by hand and re-check `--dump-config`.
113: - **The profile template decides which app you get.** A profile created with
114:   `--from-default-profile web` has no `headless` command: `dsh --profile <name> headless "task"`
115:   fails with `error: too many arguments. Expected 0 arguments but got 2: headless, task`
116:   (and `--host` is an unknown option in a `headless` profile). Recreate the profile from the
117:   template whose app you want before using that form. Reproduced on `0.2.2-rc.3` (round 8).
118: - **`subagentProvider` is a DSH subagent provider, not an LLM provider.** It must
119:   be `spawn` or `fork` (the names the profile registers through
120:   `@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent-spawn-in-process` / `-fork-in-process`). Setting it to
121:   an LLM provider id (`bifrost-completions`, …) makes every run fail closed with
122:   `no subagent provider registered for "<id>"`.
123: 
124: The settings page in the Web GUI writes into the **profile's `cordis.patch.yml`**
125: (the settings document lives there): after saving a field you can see the value in
126: that file, and it survives a restart. `roles.synthesizer`/`roles` chains are
127: rejected at load unless `synthesis: model` — the boot line names the offending key.
128: 
129: ## Activate in an existing (live) profile — needs the operator's authorisation
130: 
131: This is the checklist for moving a **running** instance onto a new build. Steps 1–4 change files
132: only; step 5 is the only one that touches a running service, and it must not be done without the
133: user saying so.
134: 
135: ```sh
136: # 1. back up the layer you are about to change
137: cp "$DSH_HOME/profiles/<name>/cordis.patch.yml" \
138:    "$DSH_HOME/profiles/<name>/cordis.patch.yml.bak-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
139: 
140: # 2. install the packed plugin. A *new path* every time: `dsh plugin add` with the same
141: #    `file:` spec is a pnpm no-op, so an unchanged path can silently keep the old contents.
142: DEST="/tmp/install-$(date +%s%N)"      # a spec this profile has never been given
143: mkdir -p "$DEST" && cp dsh-grok-workflow-0.11.18.tgz "$DEST/"
144: dsh plugin --profile <name> add "$DEST/dsh-grok-workflow-0.11.18.tgz"
145: 
146: # 3. verify the installed bytes, not the pack
147: node -p "require('$DSH_HOME/profiles/<name>/node_modules/dsh-grok-workflow/package.json').version"
148: md5sum "$DSH_HOME/profiles/<name>/node_modules/dsh-grok-workflow/lib/client.js"
149: # compare with: tar -xzOf <tgz> package/lib/client.js | md5sum
150: 
151: # 4. re-assert the bundle layer (see the reconcile boundary below) and enable a workflow provider
152: #    expected for a web profile: ["@deepseek-ai/dsh-base","@deepseek-ai/dsh-web-app","dsh-grok-workflow"]
153: #    (plus whatever other bundles the profile already had — a missing dsh-grok-workflow entry means
154: #    the layer was dropped, not that the install failed)
155: node -p "JSON.stringify(require('$DSH_HOME/profiles/<name>/package.json').dsh.profile.bundles)"
156: #   - id: workflow-ptc
157: #     config: { provider: spawn }
158: #     disabled: false
159: 
160: # 5. 🔴 RESTART THE RUNNING INSTANCE — REQUIRES THE USER'S EXPLICIT AUTHORISATION.
161: #    Never run this on a service the user is using without being asked to.
162: kill <pid from: ss -ltnp | grep :<port>>
163: DSH_HOME=/home/fish/dsh-layerfs \
164:   /home/fish/.local/bin/dsh web --host 100.111.111.88 --port 3090 --no-open   # same flags as today
165: ```
166: 
167: After the restart, prove activation with the four checks in [Enable](#enable). A settings edit
168: made later applies to the **next** message; the restart in step 5 is only needed for the plugin
169: *build* (and for a hand-edited patch file).
170: 
171: ### Why step 4 re-checks the bundle list: what `plugin add` actually does
172: 
173: `dsh plugin add` ends in `reconcile()` (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-plugin-manager/lib/index.js:326-341`),
174: which rebuilds `dsh.profile.bundles` instead of appending to it:
175: 
176: - an entry that is **not** a dependency (a bundle the launcher injects, e.g. `@deepseek-ai/dsh-base`)
177:   is kept unconditionally;
178: - an entry that **is** a dependency is kept only when the installed package still declares
179:   `dsh.bundle` (`bundleManifest(...).dsh.bundle !== undefined`);
180: - a newly installed dependency is appended only if it declares `dsh.bundle`; otherwise `dsh`
181:   prints `<name> declares no dsh.bundle — installed as a plain dependency, not a profile layer`
182:   and the package is *not* a layer.
183: 
184: So the list is not "overwritten with the new package" — it is reconciled, and the way to lose an
185: existing layer is for its installed manifest to stop declaring `dsh.bundle` (which is exactly what
186: happened in t32 when a script rewrote the installed `dsh` field) or for its dependency to be
187: removed. Both are worth catching with step 4's one-line check.
188: 
189: ## Use
190: 
191: Ask the model to call `grok_workflow` with an objective, or supply a plan:
192: 
193: ```json
194: {
195:   "objective": "Audit the repository for stale TODOs and verify each finding",
196:   "tasks": [
197:     {
198:       "id": "scan",
199:       "title": "Scan",
200:       "objective": "Find all TODO comments",
201:       "expectedOutput": "A file/line list",
202:       "acceptanceCriteria": ["Every reported path exists", "No duplicate paths"],
203:       "context": "Repository root is the working directory",
204:       "constraints": ["Do not modify files"]
205:     }
206:   ]
207: }
208: ```
209: 
210: Without `tasks`, the plugin asks a planner child to produce the plan.
211: 
212: ## Repeat runs (the composer switch)
213: 
214: The strip under the message box (`conversation.composer.dock`) carries an
215: `Auto-continue` / `自动接着跑` switch for the current session. It is the only
216: shipped control that opens a loop; the `grok_loop` tool can read and close one but
217: is refused with `loop/user-only` when it tries to open one. To check it by hand:
218: 
219: 1. open a session and look under the composer — the line reads `Checking…` (and the
220:    switch is disabled) until the first read answers, then `Off` or
221:    `On · every 60 min · 10 rounds left`;
222: 2. click once — the line names the interval and the rounds left, and
223:    `POST /grok-workflow/loop {"action":"status","sessionId":"<id>"}` answers
224:    `open: true` for that session;
225: 3. click again — the row is deleted and the same request answers `open: false`.
226: 
227: What the switch sends is what the settings page stores: `loopIntervalMin`,
228: `loopMaxRounds` and `loopFailStreak` are read when the loop opens, and the interval
229: is floored at `max(60 min, one worst-case round)`, so `loopIntervalMin: 0` means the
230: floor rather than "start now". `loopEnabled` is not read by the switch or by any
231: driver yet — it is a stored default (see the README key table).
232: 
233: Status: the request, refusal and status-line paths are covered by
234: `test/client.spec.ts` against a scripted `fetch`; the click on a live instance is
235: `NOT_RUN` as of this write-up — no DSH instance was started for it. A composition
236: with no Schedule service answers `loop/unavailable`, and the line says the Host has
237: no scheduler instead of failing silently.
238: 
239: ## Disable or uninstall
240: 
241: ```sh
242: # Disable just this row in the profile's cordis.patch.yml:
243: # - id: grok-workflow
244: #   disabled: true
245: 
246: dsh plugin --profile grok-workflow-dev remove dsh-grok-workflow
247: ```
248: 
249: The `remove` command removes the bundle and its layer.
250: 
251: ## Troubleshooting
252: 
253: - `no subagent provider registered for "spawn"`: the profile is missing
254:   `@deepseek-ai/dsh-subagent-spawn-in-process` or the engine's provider name
255:   differs. Set `provider` in the plugin config or use a profile with the base
256:   composition.
257: - `pending` plugin row `grok-workflow (…): pending (waiting for service: workflowEngine)`:
258:   the web app ships `workflow-ptc` as `disabled: true`, so nothing provides the
259:   engine. Enable it in the profile patch (see [Enable](#enable)). `--dump-config`
260:   shows the plugin row *and* the disabled provider side by side — composition is
261:   not activation.
262: - `… did not activate`: the plugin's own `resolveConfig` rejected the config and the
263:   line quotes the reason, for example
264:   `unknown configuration key "triageModel"; accepted keys: toolName, mode, grokDefault,
265:   roles, synthesis, maxConcurrency, maxTasks, timeoutMs, configVersion`, or
266:   `synthesis must be "model" or "layered", got "deterministic"`. Two stored values are
267:   *repaired* on the same line instead of being refused: `synthesis: "deterministic"`
268:   takes effect as `layered`, and `synthesis: "model"` with an empty `roles.synthesizer`
269:   chain also takes effect as `layered`.
270: - The `Grok workflow` card is missing and the browser console says
271:   `[grok-workflow] no settings namespace projects this plugin's fields`: the row did not activate
272:   (see the two lines above) or the settings service refused it. The page binds to the row that
273:   projects this plugin's fields, and says so in the console when it has to move.
274: - No `Grok workflow` card on the Plugins page although the row exists: the browser
275:   half is missing or stale. Check `<profile>/node_modules/<pkg>/lib/client.js`,
276:   `exports["./client"]` and `dsh.client` in the installed manifest; the boot HTML
277:   lists it as `dsh-grok-workflow/client.js` inside a `/plugins/??…` batch.
278: - `maximum ... active runs`: stop an in-flight workflow before starting another.
279: - Model credentials are environment-provided; never put keys in the profile,
280:   this repository, or logs.
281: 
282: ## Real-model smoke (local only)
283: 
284: Use a profile whose model route is known to work. The command must not print
285: credentials. Example shape:
286: 
287: ```sh
288: # Load the profile's environment in the shell without echoing it.
289: set -a; . ~/.dsh/bifrost.env; set +a
290: dsh --profile grok-workflow-dev headless 'Use grok_workflow ...'
291: ```
292: 
293: A freshly created isolated profile has no credential, and the run says so instead of
294: pretending: `dsh: MISSING_CREDENTIAL: llm-deepseek: no API key for provider route
295: "deepseek-official"; store DEEPSEEK_API_KEY through the credentials service …`. Never copy a
296: key out of another profile to make the smoke test pass — record the run as `BLOCKED` with that
297: line (that is what RSI round 8 did; `.rsi/evidence/round-008/`).
298: 
299: Record the exact model, profile, command, and result in
300: `docs/knowledge/VALIDATION.md`; do not record the key.
301: 
302: ## Settings identity against the real projection / 用真实投影校验设置面识别
303: 
304: The settings identity check has a manual companion that uses the DSH installation's own
305: `dsh-settings` module instead of a fixture:
306: 
307: ```sh
308: npm run build
309: node scripts/smoke-settings-identity.mjs            # discovers dsh-settings next to `dsh`
310: node scripts/smoke-settings-identity.mjs <path>     # or point at lib/types/schema.js
311: ```
312: 
313: It prints the projected field set and the diagnostics line the plugin would emit, and exits
314: non-zero when the plugin fails to recognise its own descriptor. `npm run ci` does not run it,
315: because the module belongs to the installation rather than to this package.
316: 
317: 设置面识别的手工配套检查使用 DSH 安装自带的 `dsh-settings`，而不是夹具：打印真实投影出的
318: 字段集合与插件会输出的诊断行，识别失败时以非零码退出。`npm run ci` 不跑它，因为该模块属于
319: 安装环境而不属于本包。
